newsitem.title: USA: Conrail directors meet amid reports of a settlement.
newsitem.headline: Conrail directors meet amid reports of a settlement.

text.p: Conrail Inc., widely reported to be considering splitting itself between the two railroads seeking to acquire it, said Monday that its board was meeting to review the company's options.

The meeting announcement and the reports about a possible settlement of the bitter takeover battle for the northeast railroad sent the stock of all three companies up sharply on the New York Stock Exchange.
Conrail gained $6.50 to $111, while CSX Corp. added $3.125 to $49.25 and Norfolk Sourthern Inc. tacked on $2.875 to $94.

A Conrail spokesman declined to elaborate on the options that the company's directors were considering, although several reports said the railroad's assets likely would be divided between its two suitors.
Conrail orginally agreed in October to be acquired by CSX for $9.4 billion in cash and stock but that deal was countered by a $10.5 billion cash offer from Norfolk Southern.
Norfolk Southern declined to comment on the situation Monday and CSX officials could not be reached for comment.
In January, Conrail shareholders rejected a proposal that would have permitted the CSX transaction to proceed. Many favoured Norfolk Southern's richer, all-cash offer.
Since then, the three companies have been trying to negotiate an end to the stalemate.

Sources familiar with the situation told Reuters Sunday that negotiations to end the three-way battle had gained momentum and it appeared that a negotiated deal would be struck. They said a likely deal would call for Conrail's assets to be split between CSX and Norfolk Southern.
The sources said that both CSX and Norfolk had come to realise that neither would succeed in winning Conrail alone.
Furthermore, the sources said, Conrail, which previously had opposed a division of its assets, now believed that such a scenario would be the most likely ultimate outcome.

"There has been the growing recognition that a stalemate is the worst alternative for everybody," one source close to the companies said. "The parties realise that the only way to solve it is to do something that will involve all three parties."
"It would be good for everybody involved," an expert in corporate takeovers said. "Everybody would walk away happy."
